Fractal statistical analysis under the critical point hypothesis reveals key EM signal features preceding fracture.
EM emissions studied include VLF (3 and 10 kHz) and VHF (41 and 54 MHz) bands.
Correlation coefficient r approaches values close to 1 in the last hours before failure.
Spectral amplification β shows a nearly exponential increase prior to the main event.
Local Hurst exponent h shifts from antipersistence (<0.5) to persistence (>0.5) near failure.
Loss of multifractality and narrowing of fractal dimension spectrum occur as criticality nears.
EM emission rate accelerates exponentially in the prefailure stage.
A quiescence period in EM emissions is observed about 1 hour before earthquakes.
Heterogeneity causes anisotropic damage clustering, affecting fractal properties of EM signals.
Microcracks generate acoustic and EM emissions across a wide frequency range.
Wavelet power spectrum analysis was used to study nonstationary EM signals.
Benioff cumulative EM energy release parallels mechanical strain release before earthquakes.
Power spectral density exhibits two branches corresponding to different frequency dynamics.
The fractal dimension of fault surface traces is about 1.2, while at smaller scales it is 1.6–1.7.
EM emission energy ratios correlate with radar interferometry data on fault activation.
The study analyzed data from the Kozani-Grevena earthquake (M 6.6) and the Athens earthquake (M 5.9).
The fractal dimension of the crack network decreases near final fracture stages.
EM emissions show memory effects consistent with fractal temporal correlations.
The decrease in elastic modulus near percolation threshold explains EM quiescence before rupture.
The approach to criticality is marked by an increase in the number of time intervals with fractal characteristics close to critical values.
